title: Witsuwit'en Word Salad
bodyHtml:
Witsuwit'en is a language spoken by around 3,500 people in British Columbia, Canada. Below are some sentences in Witsuwit'en and their English translations. It may be helpful to know that c', dz, gh, kw, k', lh, ts, t', y, and ' are consonants, while ë and ï are vowels.

lemidec yini'alh
He's eating a potato.
c'ighïz nildïlh
He's eating (e.g. hard-boiled) eggs.
lisuc hildïlh
He's eating sugar.
lesucam yini'alh
He's eating a turnip.
be' yi'alh
He's eating dried fish.
dïndze yini'alh
He's eating a blueberry.
tazil yi'alh
He's eating (thick) soup.
c'it'an hildïlh
He's eating leaves (e.g. kale).
c'it'an tsïlhghis yini'alh
He's eating a head of lettuce.
hida tsiy yi'alh
He's eating moose meat.
silhts'ec hildïlh
He's eating (ground) pepper.
k'inïh sigï hildïlh
He's eating cornflakes.
lhës yi'alh
He's eating a slice of bread.
cit'an hilhtsin nildïlh
He's eating onions.
ligalat yi'alh
He's eating a carrot.
c'ik'agh hildïlh
He's eating strips of bacon.

assets.alt: Illustrations of a turnip, a head of lettuce, cornflakes, rhubarb, and hazelnuts.

questions.partPrompt: For each Witsuwit'en sentence, choose the word that completes it.

questions.promptHtml: lemidec sigï ___ — He's eating a potato chip.

hints.text: There are only four possible verbs, so sort the sixteen example sentences into four groups by which verb they use. Then ask what the foods in each group have in common — not what they taste like, but what they are shaped like.

Two properties are being marked at once, and they are independent. One is roughly how many things there are, or whether the food behaves as a mass rather than a countable object. The other is about shape.

Compare dïndze yini'alh (a blueberry) with c'ighïz nildïlh (eggs). Both are round; the difference is one versus many. Now compare c'ighïz nildïlh (eggs) with c'it'an hildïlh (leaves). Both are plural; the difference is round versus not round. That gives you a two-by-two grid. Place tazil (thick soup) and lisuc (sugar) into it to see how mass nouns behave.

explanationHtml:
Witsuwit'en verbs of eating agree with the shape and number of what is being eaten. This is a classifier system, and it is common across Athabaskan languages.

The grid

non-sphericalspherical
singularyi'alhyini'alh
pluralhildïlhnildïlh

Two independent axes: singular versus plural, and roughly spherical versus not. The n in yini'alh and nildïlh marks the spherical column; the -ldïlh ending marks the plural row.

Where mass nouns land

The rule the examples establish is that granular substances count as plural, and thick substances count as singular. So sugar (lisuc hildïlh) and ground pepper (silhts'ec hildïlh) take the plural non-spherical verb — they are made of many small pieces. But thick soup (tazil yi'alh) takes the singular non-spherical verb, because it behaves as one continuous mass.

Working the answers

  • Mashed potatoes — a thick mass, not round: yi'alh.
  • French fries, rhubarb stalks, sausages, bacon strips — many long objects: hildïlh.
  • A potato chip, a cracker, a slice of bread — one flat object: yi'alh.
  • Cherries, cranberries, eggs — many round objects: nildïlh.
  • A hazelnut, a tomato, a blueberry, a turnip — one round object: yini'alh.

Notice that the noun itself does not change. All the work is done by the verb, which is why the problem title calls it a word salad: the sentence looks like a list until you realise the last word is carrying the classification.
